policy.title: Sourcing Requirements for Disseminated Analytic Products
policy.purpose: Every covered analytic product shall contain sourcing information so readers can assess the quality and credibility of sources and locate the originals. Sourcing is presented through four mechanisms: Source Reference Citations, Appended Reference Citations, Source Descriptors, and Source Summary Statements. Analysts should combine these mechanisms to optimise clarity.

rule.name: SRC required when source is cited or judgment depends on source
rule.text: A Source Reference Citation is a sequentially numbered endnote that correlates to a superscript number in the body of the analytic product. An SRC is required whenever a source is directly cited in the product text, or whenever a specific aspect of analysis (judgment, assessment, estimate, alternative hypothesis, or confidence level) depends on a source.

rule.name: SRC originality
rule.text: Reference the most original source that presents the relevant information in a form appropriate for analysis.

rule.name: SRC relevance
rule.text: The relevance of a source should be apparent if a reader consults it directly; otherwise the product text must explain the source's pertinence.

rule.name: SRC required elements
rule.text: Each SRC must include: portion marking presenting the classification; identification of the information originator, author, producer, or owner; an unambiguous source identifier enabling efficient location and retrieval; a title (with volume or issue number if applicable); date of issuance, publication, posting, or online access if unknown; page number if applicable; classification of the extracted information; and overall classification of the source document. A source descriptor may be included; if it differs from the body, the portion marking must still be included.

rule.name: ARC for supplementary information
rule.text: An Appended Reference Citation is for information that relates to analysis in a supplemental or complementary way but does not expressly affect or support a specific aspect or outcome of analysis. ARCs are optional. If included, list ARCs separately from and after SRCs. Do not include ARCs solely to delineate the overall scope of analytic inquiry.

rule.name: Source descriptor placement and content
rule.text: A source descriptor is a brief narrative about factors affecting the quality or credibility of a single source: accuracy, completeness, potential bias, relevance, age, expertise, motivation. It should appear in the main body; if not, it shall appear in the SRC. Use a source descriptor to describe qualitative factors germane to specific judgments, or when the time of the pertinent information differs significantly from the time of publication. For a directly-cited source, the descriptor should also appear in the text, clearly associated with the source.

rule.name: Source summary statement encouraged for complex products
rule.text: A source summary statement is a holistic assessment of the sourcing that supports the product as a whole. Importance increases with product complexity, source complexity, or the number of sources cited. A source summary statement should cover: strengths and weaknesses of the source base; which sources are most critical to key judgments; sources that are corroborative or conflicting; and any specific subject-matter expertise utilised.

rule.name: Dynamic and ephemeral sources
rule.text: For sources that are dynamic (e.g. an internet posting), ephemeral (e.g. an analyst phone conversation), or not subject to systematic storage, preserve a record of the source for at least one year.

rule.name: Time-horizon retention
rule.text: For products with a specified time horizon, retain source information for the time horizon or five years, whichever is shorter.

rule.name: Record copy
rule.text: Retain the covered analytic product, with all sourcing information, as a document of record, along with any downgraded, sanitised, or tearline versions.

definition.meaning: An originator or discrete parcel of data or information that contributes to, affects, or is used to evaluate intelligence analysis. A source can be a person, document, quotation, data record, database, social-media post, email, book, or web page.
The combined set of SRCs, ARCs, source descriptors, and source summary statements presented in a covered analytic product.
